systems.name: Chord Melody Harmonization System
systems.summary: The central system of the book, governing how any melody note is mapped to a chord voicing through a three-family taxonomy (Major, Minor, Dominant — with sub-families for m7b5 and altered dominant), a chord collection for every diatonic interval above a given root, and the golden rule that interval measurement is always against the current chord in the progression, not the overall key. The system's traversal logic moves the arranger horizontally across the neck via CAGED-anchored chord collections on the top two strings. Modification rules govern how voicings are altered: notes may be omitted (fifth, root, eleventh, ninth preferred), shell voicings (root, 3rd, 7th) serve as the density floor, and chords are placed sparsely — only on long-held melody notes — with unplayable voicings resolved by cutting notes rather than abandoning the chord.

members.name: Major Family
members.summary: Chords whose quality is major: CMaj7, C6, CMaj9 and extensions.

members.name: Minor m7 Sub-Family
members.summary: Minor seventh chords and extensions: Cm7, Cm9, Cm13.

members.name: Minor m7b5 Sub-Family
members.summary: Half-diminished chords: Cm7b5, Cm11b5; used on ii of minor ii-V-i.

members.name: Natural Dominant Sub-Family
members.summary: Unaltered dominant seventh chords and extensions: C7, C9, C13.

members.name: Altered Dominant Sub-Family
members.summary: Dominant chords with altered tensions: C7(b9), C7(b13b9), C7(b5), C7alt.

members.name: Chord Collection — Melody on 1st String
members.summary: Set of voicings covering every diatonic interval as the top note on the first string, organized by CAGED position.

members.name: Chord Collection — Melody on 2nd String
members.summary: Parallel set of voicings with the melody note as the highest note on the second string.

members.name: Shell Voicing
members.summary: Three-note voicing containing root, 3rd, and 7th.

traversal_rules.name: Horizontal Melody Placement on Top 2 Strings
traversal_rules.summary: Melody is repositioned onto the top 1-2 strings, requiring horizontal movement across the neck rather than staying in a single position.

references.quote_excerpt: play more horizontally over the fretboard, rather than staying in a single position
change the fingering of the melody to sit on the top 2 (or 3) strings

traversal_rules.name: CAGED-Anchored Collection Navigation
traversal_rules.summary: Navigate between chord voicings by anchoring to the CAGED fretboard area closest to the melody note.

references.quote_excerpt: play a ii V I using chord shapes from the above collections closest to each fretboard area

traversal_rules.name: Golden Rule: Interval Measured Against Current Chord
traversal_rules.summary: Select the voicing whose interval label matches the melody note's relationship to the current chord — never to the overall key.

references.topic: Golden rule: interval relates to chord
references.quote_excerpt: Always relate the interval to the chord at that point in the chord progression

references.topic: Interval label relates to current chord
references.quote_excerpt: interval number we give a melody note must relate to the current chord in the progression

traversal_rules.name: String-Set Transition Between 1st and 2nd String Collections
traversal_rules.summary: When the melody moves from the 1st to the 2nd string, transition to the corresponding 2nd-string chord collection.

references.quote_excerpt: additional chord collections that have their highest note on the 2nd string

traversal_rules.name: Chord-Scale Palette Traversal
traversal_rules.summary: Within a position, any chord from the collection may follow any other; blending chord voicings with single-note lines is the characteristic traversal gesture.

references.quote_excerpt: play through each of the shapes - any of the shapes in any order will generally sound fine
Joe Pass would often play a block chord then link to the next chord voicing with scale notes or passing tones

modification_rules.name: Shell Voicing Density Floor
modification_rules.summary: Every chord must contain at minimum the root, 3rd, and 7th — the bare bones defining chord identity.

references.quote_excerpt: shell voicings — i.e. the 'bare bones' of what you need to define the sound of the chord: the root, 3rd, and 7th
You can remove the 5th from the chord and still retain the essential character of the sound

modification_rules.name: Sparse Chord Placement — Long Notes Only
modification_rules.summary: Chords are placed only on long-held melody notes; cluttering short notes destroys melodic intelligibility.

references.quote_excerpt: I mainly place chords on the long-held melody notes
less is more — placing chords at key places 'here and there'

modification_rules.name: Note Omission Policy — 5th, Root, 11th, 9th Preferred
modification_rules.summary: When a voicing is unplayable, cut notes in order: 5th first, then root, 11th, 9th; the 3rd and 7th are kept unless the chord is especially complex.

references.quote_excerpt: Intervals most commonly omitted include the 5th, the root (1st), the 11th, and the 9th
Cut out notes from the chord - e.g. we could cut that low B to make it easier to change to the next chord

modification_rules.name: Long-Note Chord Substitution
modification_rules.summary: When a long melody note cannot ring on guitar, substitute a chord voicing to mark the harmonic change.

references.quote_excerpt: rather than trying to hold them for their full length, I place a chord voicing

modification_rules.name: Color Tone Requirement on Dominant Chords
modification_rules.summary: Extensions and altered tensions must be added to dominant chords to produce an authentically jazz-flavoured sound.

references.quote_excerpt: The jazzy sound in arrangements usually comes from adding extensions and tensions to voicings - particularly to dominant chords

modification_rules.name: Voicing Generation by Adding or Adapting Notes
modification_rules.summary: New voicings are derived from a base shape by adding or altering individual notes.

references.quote_excerpt: how many different chord voicings I can create from this G7 shape, simply by adding or adapting notes

modification_rules.name: Octave Drop for Fretboard Range Management
modification_rules.summary: When chord collection shapes climb too high on the neck, drop them an octave to stay in a practical range.

references.topic: Transposing chord collection by octave drop
references.quote_excerpt: drop some shapes down the octave when they start to get a bit too high

modification_rules.name: Sub-Family Discrimination — Altered vs Natural Dominant, m7 vs m7b5
modification_rules.summary: Sub-family selection must match the harmonic situation; the wrong sub-family produces audible harmonic errors.

references.quote_excerpt: can often sound wrong playing a natural dominant instead of an altered dominant or playing a m7 instead of a m7b5 chord

systems.name: Substitution and Reharmonization System
systems.summary: A layered substitution lattice built on top of the base harmonization system, allowing the arranger to replace or expand chords using tritone substitution (guide tones swap), relative substitution (vi for I), chord-iii substitution, minor-for-dominant (iim7 for V7), back cycling (circle of fourths), and common tone substitution (substitute chord must share the melody note). The ii/V interchangeability rule, attributed to Joe Pass, collapses two operations into a general swap freedom. Guide tones (3rd and 7th) are the harmonic engine making most substitutions valid. Lick swaps extend the system into the melodic domain by replacing repeated written melody with improvised lines matched to the underlying harmony. Back cycling and aggressive substitution are appropriate in solo guitar but may clash with other players in an ensemble.

members.name: Tritone Substitution
members.summary: Replace any chord with one whose root is a tritone away; guide tones swap positions while remaining common tones.

members.name: Relative Substitution (vi for I)
members.summary: Replace the I chord of a key with the vi chord.

members.name: Chord-iii Substitution
members.summary: Substitute a major chord for chord iii of its key.

members.name: Minor-for-Dominant Substitution (iim7 for V7)
members.summary: Use the minor 7 built on the 5th of any dominant chord in place of that dominant.

members.name: Back Cycling
members.summary: Add preparatory chords by moving backwards through the circle of fourths.

members.name: Common Tone Substitution
members.summary: Substitute any chord for another as long as the new chord shares the current melody note.

members.name: Lick Swap
members.summary: Replace a repeated melodic figure with an idiomatic jazz lick matched to the underlying harmony.

members.name: Chord Addition
members.summary: Insert substitute chords at additional points to expand harmonic rhythm.

traversal_rules.name: Guide Tone Common-Tone Validity Check
traversal_rules.summary: A substitution is valid when 3rd and 7th of the substitute are common tones with the original chord.

references.topic: guide tones swap in tritone sub
references.quote_excerpt: guide tones have essentially swapped places between these two chords

traversal_rules.name: ii-V Interchangeability
traversal_rules.summary: The ii and V chords may be freely interchanged in solo guitar arranging, attributed to Joe Pass.

references.quote_excerpt: Joe Pass would often mention that the ii and the V chord can be interchanged

traversal_rules.name: Common Tone Melody Match
traversal_rules.summary: Substitute chord must contain the current melody note as one of its chord tones.

references.quote_excerpt: substitute any chord for another chord, as long as the new chord has a note in common with it that you use as the melody note on top

traversal_rules.name: Lick Swap Structural Trigger
traversal_rules.summary: Lick swaps are triggered by a repeated melodic figure (e.g., a repeated A section) and matched to the harmonic type of that moment.

references.topic: when to substitute licks for melody
references.quote_excerpt: jazz chart with a melodic figure that repeats (e.g. a repeat of an A section) - this can be a good place to use this technique
minor ii V i progression at that point (Bm7b5 - E7(b9) - Am7), so you can use a minor ii V i jazz lick

modification_rules.name: Tritone Substitution Rule
modification_rules.summary: Any chord may be replaced by the chord whose root lies a tritone (split octave) away.

references.quote_excerpt: You can replace any chord with another whose root is a tritone away from the root of the original chord
tritone interval is sometimes referred to as a split octave

modification_rules.name: Relative Substitution Rule (vi for I)
modification_rules.summary: The I chord of a key may be replaced by the vi chord of that key.

references.quote_excerpt: you can replace the I chord of a key with the vi chord of the key

modification_rules.name: Chord-iii Substitution Rule
modification_rules.summary: A major chord may be substituted by chord iii of its key.

references.quote_excerpt: you can substitute a major chord for chord iii of its key

modification_rules.name: Minor-for-Dominant Substitution Rule
modification_rules.summary: A dominant chord may be replaced by the minor 7 chord built on its fifth scale degree.

references.quote_excerpt: You can use a minor 7 chord from the 5th of any dominant chord

modification_rules.name: Back Cycling Substitution Rule
modification_rules.summary: Additional chords may be prepended by traversing backwards through the circle of fourths; restricted to solo guitar to avoid ensemble clashes.

references.quote_excerpt: add chords to the chord progression of a song based on the 'back cycle', i.e. the circle of fourths
won't necessarily work well if you are playing in a band as the changes may clash

modification_rules.name: Late-Song Placement of Complex Substitutions
modification_rules.summary: Extreme reharmonizations should appear later in the song form so listeners first establish the original harmony.

references.quote_excerpt: may be desirable to add these kinds of substitutions a bit later in the song form

modification_rules.name: Chromatic Approach Chord
modification_rules.summary: A chromatic passing chord uses the same voicing shape one fret above or below the target chord, resolving to the target.

references.quote_excerpt: voicing on the note being approached, then play the same voicing one fret away for the approach note

systems.name: Solo Guitar Texture and Walking Bass System
systems.summary: Structural engine for solo guitar arranging: a single guitarist implies a full-band texture by rotating three layers — walking bass (strings 5-6), shell chords (downbeat or '& of 1'), and single-note melodic lines (strings 1-2). The walking bass layer has its own four-step construction rule: root on beat 1, approach note on beat 4, inner beats from scales/chromatics/arpeggios. The texture succeeds through implication and omission — the listener's mind fills in the band. Diads are preferred over octaves for richer jazz sound. The texture cycle is the book's answer to the fundamental solo guitar problem: providing bass, harmony, and melody simultaneously.

members.name: Walking Bass Layer
members.summary: Bass line on strings 5-6 with the four-step construction rule.

members.name: Shell Chord Layer
members.summary: Shell voicings dropped on downbeat or '& of 1' over the bass line.

members.name: Single-Note Melodic Line Layer
members.summary: Unaccompanied scalar lines on strings 1-2 filling space left by long melody notes.

members.name: Diad (Parallel-Interval Harmonization)
members.summary: Harmonizing a line in parallel 3rds or 6ths.

members.name: Octave Doubling
members.summary: Doubling the melody one octave below with muting of the intervening string.

members.name: Arpeggiation
members.summary: Notes of a chord plucked one at a time for a lyrical effect, especially in ballads.

traversal_rules.name: Texture Rotation — Illusion of Full Band
traversal_rules.summary: Alternate between walking bass, chord lines, and single-note lines across measures to create the illusion of a rhythm section.

references.quote_excerpt: alternating through these different devices gives the 'illusion' to the audience of a complete band

traversal_rules.name: Walking Bass as Long-Note Fill
traversal_rules.summary: Deploy walking bass specifically during long-held melody notes to maintain rhythmic drive.

references.quote_excerpt: walking bass is used to fill out sections where there is a long-held melody note

traversal_rules.name: Shell Voicing Rhythmic Placement — Downbeat or & of 1
traversal_rules.summary: Shell voicings placed on beat 1 or '& of 1' to create rhythmic variety.

references.quote_excerpt: It's good to mix up playing them on the downbeat and on the '& of 1' to create variety

traversal_rules.name: Diad Preference Over Octaves
traversal_rules.summary: Diads (parallel 3rds or 6ths) preferred over octaves for a richer, more authentic jazz sound.

references.quote_excerpt: alternative approach to using octaves and is a softer but richer sound, which sounds very authentic in the jazz guitar tradition
Diads are when you harmonize a line in a parallel interval, usually 3rds or 6ths

modification_rules.name: Walking Bass Four-Step Construction
modification_rules.summary: Build a walking bassline: (1) root on beat 1, (2) approach note on beat 4, (3-4) inner beats from scales, chromatics, or arpeggios.

references.quote_excerpt: Place the root on beat 1 of each bar
add either a diatonic or chromatic note on beat 4
add two more notes in between the root note of beat 1, and the approach note of beat 4

modification_rules.name: Bass String Prominence in Solo Arrangement
modification_rules.summary: In solo guitar, strings 5-6 must carry the bass function; arrangement sounds thin without it.

references.topic: Bass notes role in solo guitar
references.quote_excerpt: no longer have a bass player to play with, so you need to fill that role ourselves

modification_rules.name: Key Selection for Open-String Bass Notes
modification_rules.summary: Choose an arrangement key (A, E, D) that allows open strings on the bass, freeing fretting fingers.

references.quote_excerpt: Choosing a key like A, E, or D gives you essentially another set of free fingers

modification_rules.name: Arpeggiation in Ballad Context
modification_rules.summary: Substitute block chord plucking with arpeggiation in ballad arrangements for a lyrical texture.

references.quote_excerpt: Arpeggiation is when you pluck the notes of a chord one at a time
